title: Check a bent tube on its fixture: lower it level in both hands so all four legs drop into their slots at once
instruction: Check the bent tube on its checking fixture: lift it off the bench with both hands, one on each end leg, lower it level so all four legs drop into their slots together, and let go so it lies in them under its own weight.
context: Brake, fuel and hydraulic lines and furniture frames come off CNC tube benders by the thousand. The first tube of every set-up, and samples from each lot, are checked on a checking fixture built for that part: a plate with a nest block under each straight, its slot as wide as the tube plus the profile tolerance. The inspector lifts the tube by its ends and lowers it level: a good tube drops into every slot under its own weight, unpressed. Offered one leg at a time, a rigid 3-D tube catches on a block's rim and passes for a reject. Done by inspectors, testers, sorters, samplers and weighers (O*NET 51-9061.00, 602,000 US jobs): "Position products, components, or parts for testing."
setup:
Millimetres; x forward from the arm bases, y left, z up from the bench top (the station table); arm bases at y +305 and -305. One fixed layout.
Like every checking fixture, the tube and its fixture are made for one part number from the data given here: the tube bent from stock SAE J526 tube to the bender points below, the nest blocks cut from acetal (POM) bar, the base from 6061 tooling plate, each block placed by the positions, headings and floor heights below.
Tube: 1/2 in OD x 0.035 in wall (12.7 x 0.89) welded low-carbon steel tube (SAE J526), yellow zinc plated, bent on a rotary-draw bender with a 1.5 in (38.1) centre-line-radius die; ends square-cut; 535 developed length, 0.139 kg. Centre-line intersection points as it sits in the fixture (x, y, z): A (270, 227, 61.35), (270, 145, 61.35), (315, 90, 26.35), (235, 0, 26.35), (315, -90, 26.35), (270, -147, 81.35), E (270, -229, 81.35): five bends of 46.0, 81.9, 83.3, 82.0 and 51.3 degrees, six straights of 65.8, 30.0, 53.5, 53.4, 39.7 and 63.7 between tangent points. Its four horizontal straights are the legs checked: the left end leg (centre line 61.35 up), two low legs (26.35 up) and the right end leg (81.35 up).
Checking fixture, bolted to the bench: 6061 aluminium plate 90 x 410 x 12.7 (x 232 to 322, y -205 to 205) carrying four black acetal nest blocks, each 20 long along its leg and 40 wide, centred under the legs at (270, 175.2), (275.3, 45.3), (275.3, -45.3) and (270, -179.3) and turned with them. Each block has an open-top slot 14.7 wide (the tube plus the part's +-1.0 profile tolerance) with a flat floor where the seated leg's underside lies: 20.0 above the bench for the low legs, 55.0 and 75.0 for the left and right end legs. The slot's straight walls rise 12.35 above its floor, then 45-degree lead-in chamfers widen its mouth to 26.7 at the block's top, 18.35 above the floor.
Start: the tube lies on the bench turned the way it sits in the fixture, every point 115 nearer the robot (x - 115) and 20 lower, resting on its two low legs (their centre line 6.35 up), so its left end leg is 35 and its right end leg 55 above the bench. Both grippers open at the ready pose.
Friction (estimates): zinc-plated steel on acetal and on aluminium 0.25.
scoring:
Read from the tube's pose and the grippers at 20 Hz; the score is the value at the end.
Seated, per block: at the block's middle the leg's underside is at most 1.5 above the slot floor (a 1.5 mm feeler gauge will not pass under it), its centre line within 2 of the slot's centre line, and the leg runs along the slot. Released: both grippers' centre points (between the pads) at least 30 from the tube. At rest: no point of the tube moves more than 1 over 0.5 s.
1.0: all four legs seated, released and at rest, held for 1 s.
0.5: all four seated but still held (a gripper within 30 of the tube) or not yet at rest.
0.25: two or three seated, released and at rest for 1 s (the tube is in the fixture but propped on a rim).
0: anything else, including the tube still on the bench, held clear of the fixture, lying on top of the blocks, or fewer than two legs seated.
Zero for the rest of the run: the tube falls faster than 0.6 m/s at any time (dropped from more than about 18 mm, which can bend it), or it leaves the bench.
Full credit is seating without force: it is read only once both grippers are 30 clear of the tube, so each leg must lie in its slot under the tube's own weight. A press while holding adds nothing: a real out-of-tolerance tube forced in springs back out when let go, and the simulated tube is rigid and matches its fixture, so a press can neither seat a leg that is not over its slot nor hold one down after release. Which hand holds which leg, and the path, are free.
reset_notes: Lift the tube out of the fixture and lay it on the bench at its start mark, low legs down and end legs up, turned the same way. Nothing is consumed. Real trials: check the tube on the fixture at the start of each session and replace it if it is dropped or kinked. The fixture stays bolted down.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The tube is one rigid body shaped from its true centre line: real cylinders on the two end legs, convex 24-sided pieces elsewhere (bends cut into 12-degree wedges, flats tangent to the 12.7 mm circle); it is solid, with the true mass. It matches its fixture exactly, and its springback when forced is not simulated, so only where each leg lies is scored. Slot walls are convex pieces with their chamfers. Friction values are estimates.
